messages.content: Summarize why reproducible ML experiments need pinned dependencies.

Pinned dependencies (fixing exact package versions) are essential for reproducible ML experiments because they freeze the software environment so future runs produce the same behaviour and results. Key reasons:

- Deterministic code paths: Small library changes (new defaults, bugfixes, or altered algorithms) can change training or evaluation behavior. Pinning prevents unintentional code-path or logic drift.
- Stable APIs and semantics: Upgrading a dependency can change function signatures, parameter meanings, numerical stability, or randomness handling; exact versions avoid surprises.
- Numerical reproducibility: Differences in numerical libraries (BLAS/LAPACK, NumPy, PyTorch/TensorFlow) and their builds (compiler, CPU/GPU kernels) affect floating-point results. Pinning narrows one source of variability.
- Dependency graph control: Transitive dependency updates can introduce incompatible or subtly different packages. Explicit pins lock the whole graph and avoid silent upgrades.
- Easier debugging and provenance: When results are tied to specific versions, you can reproduce, compare, and debug experiments reliably and attribute changes to code/data rather than shifting libraries.
- Environment recreation and CI: Pins enable exact recreation of environments locally, in containers, and in continuous-integration systems, making experiments portable and automatable.
- Compliance and auditability: For regulated or long-lived projects, pinned environments provide an auditable, repeatable record of the software used.

Caveats and best practices:
- Pin at an appropriate granularity (top-level and key scientific libs; consider lockfiles for full graph).
- Record runtime platform details (OS, CPU/GPU, drivers, CUDA/cuDNN) because pins alone don’t capture
